analysis.one_liner: Bans federal oil and gas drilling permits within 1,500 feet of homes, schools, and businesses.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died in the House Natural Resources Committee when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Mineral Leasing Act, the law governing oil and gas development on federal lands, to bar the Interior Department from approving any drilling operation within 1,500 feet of a home, business, school, or other building the Secretary determines needs special protection. Setback rules like this are meant to keep drilling noise, truck traffic, air emissions, and spill risk away from where people live and learn. It applied only to federally issued permits, not to drilling authorized solely under state or private rules.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or go to school near potential federal drilling sites, especially in communities already surrounded by oil and gas operations; they would get a legally enforceable 1,500-foot buffer between new drilling and occupied buildings.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Interior Department from issuing permits for any oil and gas drilling operation located within 1,500 feet of a home, business, school, or other building requiring special protection, as determined by the Secretary.
Creates the buffer by amending the Mineral Leasing Act, so the setback applies to drilling operations that depend on federal permitting authority.

The bill lists schools and other buildings requiring special protection first in the text, and the named cosponsors came largely from urban and suburban districts in California, Texas, and Florida where neighborhoods sit close to oil fields.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies operating on federal leases, which would lose the ability to site new wells within 1,500 feet of occupied buildings; some leases near populated areas could become unusable, reducing production and federal drilling revenue from those tracts.

drawbacks.text: The 1,500-foot distance applies only to permits issued by the Interior Department under the Mineral Leasing Act, so drilling authorized purely under state or private rules would remain unaffected, leaving an uneven patchwork of protection depending on who owns the land.

The buffer could make some federal leases uneconomic to develop, reducing domestic oil and gas output from tracts near towns and cities and the federal revenue that comes with them; an honest supporter would acknowledge that trade-off.

The phrase 'other building that requires special protection, as determined by the Secretary' gives the Interior Department broad discretion, which critics could argue creates uncertainty for operators about where the line falls.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people living next to drilling sites, a setback delivers clear health, safety, and quality-of-life protections at little direct cost to them. The cost falls on operators who lose flexibility near populated areas and on energy production from those specific tracts. The bill's main design weakness is its limited reach: because it covers only federal permits, protection would depend on land ownership rather than on where people actually live.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Nanette Barragan introduced the bill on November 3, 2017, with eight original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources the same day.
On November 14, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, its last recorded action.
The bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action in the House or Senate before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
The CRS summary confirms the bill's single substantive provision: a prohibition on Interior Department drilling permits within 1,500 feet of homes, businesses, schools, or other protected buildings.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas operators on federal leases are better off, since nothing now stops the Interior Department from permitting new wells within 1,500 feet of homes and schools; residents near drilling sites got no buffer.

for.name: Rep. Nanette Diaz Barragan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor.

for.name: 9 House cosponsors
for.role: Reps. Lee, Khanna, Roybal-Allard, Gomez, Soto, Grijalva, Evans, and Ellison (original cosponsors) plus one later cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 10 Democratic supporters in the House.

against.name: Rep. Rob Bishop
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or hearing on the bill, leaving it stuck in its subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 House supporters were Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors; the Republican-led Natural Resources Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies operating on federal leases
industries.note: The bill would bar Interior from permitting new drilling within 1,500 feet of homes, businesses, and schools, removing the option to site wells next to occupied buildings. Companies benefit from keeping that option, while residents near sites bear the noise, traffic, emissions, and spill risk.

industries.industry: Homeowners and communities near drilling areas
industries.note: A setback rule gives residents near federal drilling sites a buffer from new wells, though only for federally permitted operations.
